segments.line: You wake up and the world has changed.
Above every head, a little green label.
Everyone's biggest allergy, written where only you can see it.
The labels glow softly in the morning light. Peanuts on the construction worker three buildings over.
Pollen on the jogger running past the window.
Cats on the woman with the baby stroller two doors down.
You pull your hoodie up, checking your own head.
No label, just skin.
You're the only one who doesn't have a tag.
The labels are different for everyone.
Some are small, some are bold,
but they're all there above every head while yours stands alone.
It's a quiet morning. The sun is just coming up.
People are starting their day, but the labels are already there.
Peanuts on the construction worker, pollen on the jogger,
cats on the woman with the baby stroller.
On the bus, the big guy's label says peanuts.
The girl by the window, pollen.
Even the driver, cats.
The labels never lie. They don't change.
And nobody else can see them. Only you.
You watch the labels float above the crowd.
Each one, a secret you now hold.
A responsibility you never asked for.
What if you could read anyone's allergies?
Not just the big ones, not just the obvious ones.
Every single one. All day, every day.
Labels above every head. Sounds like a superpower, right?
Stick around, because by the end of this,
it won't feel like one.
First, the rules.
The labels appear above every head. Green, rounded rectangle stamps with white, bold caps.
They show each person's biggest allergy.
They never lie. They don't change.
And nobody else can see them. Only you.
Your own head has no label. You can't see your own allergy.
The labels are about big allergies, the ones that cause real reactions,
not mild sensitivities. The ones that make you break out in hives,
that make you gasp for air, that make you carry an EpiPen.
